title: Star stuff
hookLine: Carl Sagan: we are made of star stuff
carry: the cosmos has a way to know itself

cards: The nearest object to you right now is probably your own hand. Skin, knuckles, the faint lines on the palm, the blue of a vein at the wrist. It goes everywhere you go, and it's easy to stop seeing it.

The astronomer Carl Sagan, in his television series and book Cosmos, said something about what that hand is made of, something that sounds like poetry but was meant as plain fact. We are made, he said, of star stuff.

teach.b: Sagan's words are paraphrased here, not quoted. First, the claim.
In Cosmos, Sagan explained that the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, even the carbon in an apple pie, were made inside stars.
Much of what our bodies are built from was forged in stars and scattered when they died. Second, what that does to distance. Pascal looked at the stars and felt the silence of the infinite spaces.
Sagan looks at the same stars and sees family.
Some of the sky is here, in the hand nearest you. Third, the next step.
Through us, Sagan said, the cosmos has a way to know itself. The stuff of stars, put together as a person, looks back up and wonders where it came from. Fourth, a neighbor's line.
In Genesis, God tells Adam: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's a different teaching, from a different source, and Sagan wasn't quoting it.
But some readers hold the two side by side: dust, and star stuff. Both say a person is made of the stuff of the world, and some hear in both a call to humility, and to wonder.

how: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, use Sagan's picture of star stuff as a short contemplation on the body, often looking at a hand or feeling the pulse while recalling where its materials came from.

o: Sagan's phrase for the dust and gas floating between galaxies
a poet's name for the light of stars that died long ago
Sagan's phrase for what we're made of: elements forged inside stars

s: Sagan said elements in our bodies, like iron and calcium, were made inside stars
nitrogen, calcium, iron, carbon: he said they were made inside stars.
the phrase star stuff comes from the Bible
it's Sagan's phrase, from Cosmos; Genesis says "dust thou art."
Sagan's point was that people are too small to matter
he said that through us the cosmos has a way to know itself.

games.q: Carl Sagan looks at a human body. where does he say the calcium in its teeth and the iron in its blood were made?
games.why: Sagan said they were made inside stars, and that we are made of star stuff.

practice: Rest one hand palm up in your lap or on a table, and look at it as if you'd never seen it: the lines, the color, the pulse at the wrist if you can find it.
Let the thought come once, without forcing it: much of this was made inside stars. Then just keep looking, and breathing.

wordCard.voice: Star stuff. Carl Sagan's phrase for what we're made of: materials made inside stars, now able to look back up and wonder. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the cosmos has a way to know itself. Dust, and star stuff, looking back up. Until tomorrow.
